title: A double-integral region cut two ways: does the order of integration matter?
summary: The same region is sliced into vertical strips on the left and horizontal strips on the right. Each way gives its own limits of integration; for a well-behaved integrand both orders give the same value.

media.alt: Two copies of a leaf-shaped region between y = x^2 and y = sqrt(x). Left: ten vertical teal strips with one amber. Right: ten horizontal blue strips with one amber. Under each panel the double integral is typeset with its limits.
media.caption: Reference render of class F3.4 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data. Standard theory only.

read_the_figure.question: Does order of integration matter?
read_the_figure.axes: Both panels: x and y from 0 to 1.1, equal scale. The region is bounded below by y = x^2 and above by y = sqrt(x). Left strips run vertically (dy inside, dx outside), right strips horizontally (dx inside, dy outside). Amber marks one strip in each panel.
look_at: For the left strips, what are the limits of x and of y?
For the right strips, what are the limits of y and of x?
Why do the two panels look like mirror images?
Do both orders give the area 1/3?
as_drawn: The limits are written under each panel: left x from 0 to 1 and y from x^2 to sqrt(x); right y from 0 to 1 and x from y^2 to sqrt(y).
The region is symmetric under swapping x and y (the curve y = x^2 is the mirror of x = y^2), which is why the strips mirror each other.
The note at the bottom says the area is 1/3 both ways. The typeset integral overlaps the x tick label in this render, a layout flaw.
read_the_figure.proves: That the limits can be written both ways for this region and that, for f = 1, both give 1/3. It does not prove equality for other integrands: that requires Fubini's conditions.
if_wrong: No limits written: the reader cannot reproduce the integral.
Strips drawn but one direction impossible for the region (a region that needs splitting): the figure hides that.
Region plotted with unequal axes: the area looks wrong.

terms.meaning: A sum over a plane region of f times small area elements.
An integral done in two steps: first over the inner variable, then over the outer.
The bounds of each variable; the inner ones may depend on the outer variable.
If f is integrable (for example continuous on a bounded region) the order of integration does not change the result.

terms.term: Type I and type II region
terms.meaning: A region described as y between two curves of x (vertical strips) or x between two curves of y (horizontal strips).
A small piece of area, dx dy.

remember: Draw the strip first; the limits read off the strip's ends.
Inner limits may depend on the outer variable; outer limits are constants.
Swap order: redraw the region and read new limits.
Fubini holds for continuous integrands on a bounded region, not for every integrand.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: The region is a shaded area; its boundary lines are curves. Strips are rectangles whose long side points along the inner variable. The amber strip is one example, and the typeset integral under each panel gives the limits that the strip implies.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: The integral is a sum of area elements, and a strip is the way you group them. Cut into vertical strips, the inner integral runs in y with limits that depend on x; cut into horizontal strips, the roles swap. The figure shows that these are two ways of covering one region, which explains why the answer should be the same, and why the limits change.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: The strips drawn are finite; the integral uses the limit of vanishing width. Region shapes that need splitting in one order (a region with a dent) are easy cases not shown. The figure can't show when Fubini fails (an integrand that is not absolutely integrable). And unequal axes distort areas.

understand.title: Why each required item matters
understand.text: Both strip directions let the reader see that the order is a choice. Labelled limits make the picture an integral you could compute. A region that is symmetric, like this one, hides how hard a swap can be for other regions.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: For circular regions use polar strips (rays and arcs). For a numerical check use Monte Carlo or a fine grid. If one order is hard, as for sin(y^2), swap order: the figure shows how the region looks in each.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Add a region where one order needs two integrals (for example a triangle with a notch) and show the split strips; add the value of the integral next to each limit set.

steps.title: The limits both ways
steps.note: The curves y = x^2 and y = sqrt(x) meet at (0, 0) and (1, 1). Solving each for the other variable gives x = sqrt(y) and x = y^2, so the horizontal-strip limits are y^2 to sqrt(y).

steps.title: The area both ways
steps.note: Checked numerically to 1e-16. For f = 1 the two orders give the area, 1/3.

worked.title: Reading the reference render
worked.problem: From the figure: (1) what are the limits for vertical strips? (2) For horizontal strips? (3) How wide is the amber strip in the left panel and how tall is it?

solution.text: x runs from 0 to 1 and, at each x, y runs from x^2 to sqrt x.
y runs from 0 to 1 and, at each y, x runs from y^2 to sqrt y.
The amber strip is at x about 0.45, height sqrt(0.45) - 0.45^2 = 0.67 - 0.20 = 0.47, with a width of 0.1 (ten strips).

worked.answer: Left: x in [0, 1], y in [x^2, sqrt x]. Right: y in [0, 1], x in [y^2, sqrt y]. Both orders give area 1/3.

checks.q: What changes when you swap the order of integration for a region?
checks.answer: The limits are re-read from the region: the inner limits are now functions of the other variable. The value is unchanged for a continuous integrand.

checks.q: The region is between y = x^2 and y = sqrt x. What is its area?
An iterated integral gives pi/4 in one order and -pi/4 in the other. Does that contradict Fubini?
checks.answer: No: Fubini's theorem requires the integrand to be absolutely integrable; for the standard counter-example it is not, so the orders may disagree.
